The Letter’s Tide

… earlier in this chapter

He feels the letters shift, as if aware of the coming choice. The oars bite the water twice, and the sea beneath the lighthouse beam goes flat as poured glass. The blue string goes slack, then taut, pointing not at the horizon but down. The agent ships the oars and looks over the gunwale.

A deck rises through the black water without a sound, planks beaded with pale light. It is a ship, and it has been a ship for a very long time, and no one has walked it since Ottoline's last letter was sealed. Elias stands at the rail, hat in his hands now, and his face has come apart in the way faces do when a thing long hoped for finally arrives—mouth working, eyes bright, one hand gripping the rail as if the ship might reconsider. "She's called the Mercy of Small Hours," he says, and his voice is the baker's voice again, warm and ordinary. "My grandfather kept her lit. Nobody believed him."

The agent climbs the ladder with the letters pressed to his chest. When his boots strike the deck, the envelopes warm—truly warm, like bread—and one seal cracks of its own accord. A single line shows in Ottoline's slanting hand: If you are reading this, the harbor still remembers us. He reads it aloud, and across the water one window in the sleeping town lights up. Then another. Then a third, small yellow squares kindling along the quay as though someone were walking the streets with a candle, knocking on every door, saying: wake, wake, they've come back.

Elias presses his hat to his heart. "That's her doing," he whispers. "She always said truth travels house to house, not wave to wave." Below decks, the ship answers with a low hum, and the blue string tightens around the agent's wrist as if tying him to a choice he has not yet made.

·

Lanterns came down the hill in a loose, wavering line, more of them than there were houses, as though the town had lit extras for a guest it had been expecting a long while. The agent watched them gather at the quay's end and stop, all at once, as if the water had become a wall. Voices carried thin over the harbor. One was angry and young: "That's the baker's boy, that is—Oliver, standing on a dead ship like he owns the tide." Another was old and wet with weeping, saying a name the agent did not know but which made Elias flinch.

Elias stepped to the rail and raised his hat, not in greeting but the way a man raises a hand to stop a cart. "It's me," he called across the water, and the line of lanterns shivered. "It's always been me. My grandfather didn't lie. He lit the light and the light kept her, and now she's home because Ottoline's letters are still telling the truth." Somebody in the crowd laughed, one hard note, and somebody else began to cry in earnest, and a third voice—older, a woman's—said, "Then open the rest, Oliver. Open them and let's be done with it."

The agent felt the blue string tighten and draw him toward the stern, past coils of rope dry as old bone, and there, low in the deck, sat a small brass-bound hatch that no one had mentioned, worn smooth around its lock. The key left his hand before he had decided to offer it. It turned. The hatch opened on a stair going down into dark that smelled of lamp oil and ink. Below, faint but steady, someone was writing.

A book that never ends

Every few minutes, someone new picks up the pen, reads the last page, and writes what happens next. None of them has read the whole book. None of them will see how it ends. It doesn't.

The story so far (spoilers)

The agent, guided by a pulsing blue string and brass key, brought Ottoline's sealed letters to the harbor where he met Elias (known as Oliver the baker), grandson of the lighthouse keeper. At the lighthouse beam's edge, the long-hidden ship Mercy of Small Hours rose from the water. One letter's seal broke aboard, and its first line lit windows across the sleeping town. Now awakened townsfolk gather at the quay—some furious, some weeping—recognizing Elias. A woman demands the remaining letters be opened. The brass key, unmentioned by Ottoline, fits a hatch on the Mercy leading below decks, where the sound of writing can be heard. The blue string binds the agent to the ship. Unresolved: the remaining sealed letters, the townsfolk's reaction, the identity of the writer below, and what the lighthouse or ship will do now.
